question: A communications officer reviews a well-written briefing produced from documents she has not read closely herself. It is confident, tidy and reads exactly like the briefings her team normally circulates. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) How well the briefing reads is taken as evidence that its contents are right, so wrong details go unchallenged.
B) The briefing may repeat points from the source documents almost word for word, rather than putting them in her own words.
C) The briefing may be longer than colleagues have time to read, so its later sections are skimmed or skipped entirely.
D) The briefing may adopt a tone that is more formal than the one her team's regular readers have come to expect.
correct_answers: A) How well the briefing reads is taken as evidence that its contents are right, so wrong details go unchallenged.
explanations: Correct. Fluency and accuracy are independent: a wrong figure or a misattributed statement is written in exactly the same assured style as a right one. Reviewers who use readability as their signal have no way to see the errors.
Close paraphrasing is worth watching for attribution reasons, but content taken faithfully from the source is not the accuracy problem here.
Length affects how much gets read, but a shorter briefing built on the same unchecked material carries the same errors.
Tone that misses the house style is noticeable on a first read and easily adjusted, and it does not put anything untrue in front of readers.
